<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases, but PRO controlled the decisive thread of the debate. PRO's framing — that the motion already carves out material business harm, leaving only the question of whether "irrelevant" firings deserve protection — forced CON to either name a genuinely job-irrelevant case worth firing over or concede the point. CON's Pressure Questions answer (the gambling bookkeeper, the reputational-risk hire) redefined "irrelevant" as latent, unproven risk rather than answering the question as posed, and PRO's closing exploited this cleanly, showing CON's standard collapses into unlimited managerial discretion that "cannot distinguish prudence from prejudice." CON's strongest material — the vagueness of "material" and the asymmetry between quitting and firing — was answered with a workable analogy to existing legal standards (BFOQ, undue hardship, negligence) and with the sharp point that CON already accepts categorical, judgment-laden carve-outs (race, whistleblowing) while claiming symmetry must be absolute elsewhere, a real internal tension CON never fully resolved. CON's closing dilemma ("exception swallows the rule, or paralysis") was a decent late move but arrived without engaging PRO's standing analogy to functioning legal tests, and its retreat toward severance/UI as a consolation implicitly conceded that firing itself needed no justification, which PRO seized on. Both openings suffered word-limit clipping near the end, but the lost material was largely restated elsewhere and affected both sides symmetrically.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 in Pressure Questions (name a lawful, off-duty, genuinely job-irrelevant case still deserving firing) and CON's evasive answer via the gambling-bookkeeper/reputational-risk examples, which PRO's closing exposed as redefining "irrelevant" into "unproven risk" — collapsing CON's own materiality standard.</best_rebuttal>
